newsitem.title: JAPAN: N.Korea reports Kim appearance, soothes fears.
newsitem.headline: N.Korea reports Kim appearance, soothes fears.

text.p: In an apparent bid to dampen speculation of a power struggle, North Korean media on Sunday reported the first public appearance by its leader Kim Jong-il since the defection of a senior Pyongyang official 11 days ago.
A broadcast by official Pyongyang Radio, monitored by Tokyo-based Radiopress, reported that Kim attended a mass gymnastics display last Thursday.
Radiopress said it was the first mention in North Korea's official media of a public appearance by Kim since February 4 when he attended a youth concert.
In the past 11 days, North Korea has been rocked by leadership changes in which three of its 25 top leaders have departed from the power structure.

The communist country's premier was replaced, the defence minister died and in the greatest blow Pyongyang's ideology chief Hwang Jang-yop defected to the South Korean consulate in Beijing on February 12.
Outgoing premier Kang Song-san, 66, was replaced last Friday and Defence minister Choe Kwang, 78, died of a heart attack on the same day.
Choe was ranked sixth, Kang seventh and Hwang 24th in the Stalinist nation's power structure.
"The report of Kim's appearance is a signal by North Korea that despite changes he is still in charge," a Radiopress analyst said.

The sudden leadership changes come as North Korea struggles to survive a famine caused by two consecutive years of floods and negotiates with the United States and other western nations for both food and the possible start of peace talks.

Kim, although already in effective control of the North, has yet to take over the key posts held by his father Kim Il-sung, the founder of North Korea -- those of state president and general secretary of the ruling party.
There is speculation he would formally assume the titles after the third anniversary of his father's death in July.
In hopes of ending food shortages Kim last Friday agreed to take part in a briefing by the United States and South Korea on their proposal for four-nation Korean peace talks, that also include China.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeline Albright, who was visiting South Korea, said on Saturday that the success of Korean peace talks depended heavily on how desparate Pyongyang was economically.
She was slated to fly to Japan early on Sunday for the next leg of her Asian tour.
Pyongyang's agreement to attend the briefing in New York on March 5 follows promises by Washington and Seoul to send $10 million and $6 million respectively in food aid to the North.

The United States and South Korea proposed the talks as a way to eventually bring about a permanent peace on the Korean peninsula. The two Koreas remain technically at war since their 1950-53 conflict ended in a truce, not a peace pact.
